claims.text: The damaged turbine blade is made from a nickel-based superalloy such as Inconel 718.
The blade's damage and microstructural degradation make fusion-welding repair unsuitable because of hot-cracking risk.
Localized FSP can repair the damaged region while keeping the processed material below its melting temperature.
FSP can be performed on this nickel-based superalloy at approximately 0.6–0.8 Tm under high pressure.
Advanced tool-path control can confine the FSP repair zone.
Friction stir processing induces dynamic recrystallization in the repair zone.
Dynamic recrystallization produces a refined and homogeneous grain structure in the processed zone.
Localized FSP preserves the surrounding, unprocessed microstructure.
Severe plastic deformation from the FSP tool causes dynamic recrystallization without melting.
Avoiding melting eliminates liquid-phase solidification and thereby eliminates fusion-related hot cracking.
The combination of localized heat and mechanical energy creates a fine-grained, mechanically robust repair microstructure.
The FSP repair zone will have fatigue, wear, and creep resistance comparable to or superior to the base material.
The FSP repair will improve fatigue, creep, and wear resistance relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
The FSP repair will significantly reduce hot-cracking propensity relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
Traditional fusion-welding repair suffers from hot cracking because of prolonged high-temperature exposure and liquid-phase solidification.
Fusion-welding repair produces inferior microstructural integrity and mechanical performance.
FSP repair is limited to components with accessible damaged zones and sufficiently precise parameter control.

contradictions.description: The rule equates a statistically significant improvement with 'equal or higher' performance. Equality is not a statistically significant improvement, so the stated criterion is internally inconsistent.
